AN OPEN LETTER TO MA'AM LOTIS, MA'AM RUTH, AND MA'AM GINA OF THE NURSING DEPARTMENTTo Ma'am Lotis, Ma'am Ruth, and Ma'am Gina,I am writing this open letter to express my disappointment and serious concern regarding the Focus Group Discussion (FGD) conducted last Wednesday. What was supposed to be an opportunity for students to express their honest opinions and provide constructive feedback appeared, from our perspective, to become an interrogation directed toward finding faults in one particular professor: Sir Carlo Roy Roslinda.Let me make one thing clear: students are entitled to express their concerns, and professors are not exempt from constructive criticism. However, feedback should be gathered fairly, objectively, and without creating an atmosphere where students feel pressured to say something negative about a particular faculty member.During the FGD, the discussion appeared to revolve heavily around Sir Carlo, particularly regarding the concern that he dismisses his students earlier than the officially scheduled class dismissal time. While this matter may be worth discussing, I believe it is equally important to consider the circumstances. There are instances when lessons and discussions have already been completed. If the learning objectives have been achieved and there are no remaining activities, should a professor automatically be judged negatively for dismissing the class early? Is the number of minutes spent inside the classroom a more important measure of teaching effectiveness than the actual knowledge and understanding students gain?Sir Carlo is one of the professors whom we genuinely appreciate. His ability to explain complicated Anatomy and Physiology concepts, make discussions understandable, and help students appreciate the subject is something that should not be overlooked. Anatomy and Physiology is not an easy subject, especially for first-year nursing students. Yet, his teaching approach has helped many of us understand topics that would otherwise be difficult to comprehend.What was particularly concerning during the FGD was the impression that questions were being directed toward students to uncover weaknesses in Sir Carlo's teaching. For instance, Ma'am Gina asked students about the different parts of the Fallopian tube and subsequently asked about the functions of those structures. There is absolutely nothing wrong with assessing students' knowledge. However, in the context of the discussion, the questioning gave the impression that students were being tested to find grounds for criticizing a professor rather than being genuinely asked about their learning experience.An FGD should never feel like an examination designed to expose a professor's supposed shortcomings. It should be a safe and impartial environment where students can share both positive and negative experiences without feeling intimidated, influenced, or pressured.More importantly, character assassination should never be mistaken for professional evaluation. There is a significant difference between identifying areas for improvement and creating a discussion that appears intended to damage someone's professional reputation. If there are legitimate concerns about a professor, they should be addressed through proper evaluation, objective evidence, and an opportunity for the concerned faculty member to explain his side.I also want to raise a broader concern regarding the working and learning environment within the Nursing Department. From the experiences and observations of students, concerns about the department's culture and handling of faculty and student matters have existed since 2025. This should not simply be dismissed as students being overly sensitive or unwilling to accept criticism. When multiple students begin questioning the department's approach to communication, leadership, and professionalism, perhaps it is time for the administration to listen and reflect.To the Nursing Department, I hope you understand that students do not attend university merely to comply with schedules, complete requirements, and receive grades. We are here to learn, develop our competence, and become future healthcare professionals. We deserve an environment where our opinions are respected and where our professors are evaluated based on fairness, competence, and the quality of education they provide.We are not asking for professors to be immune from criticism. We are asking for consistency. If students are expected to demonstrate professionalism, respect, and accountability, the same standards should apply to everyone, regardless of their position or title.I sincerely hope that the Dean and the university administration will take these concerns seriously and conduct an impartial review of the Nursing Department's leadership and internal practices. If necessary, I hope they will consider leadership changes and the replacement of individuals whose continued handling of departmental matters has contributed to a loss of student trust.A department cannot promote professionalism while allowing its own practices to contradict the values it expects students to uphold.Lastly, I want to express my appreciation for Sir Carlo Roy Roslinda. Good professors deserve recognition, not an environment where their dedication is overshadowed by personal disagreements or questionable evaluation practices. A professor's worth should be measured by the knowledge he imparts, the students he inspires, and the positive impact he creates in the classroom.We are nursing students. We are learning to become advocates for our future patients, and that advocacy should begin with having the courage to speak up when we believe something is unfair.I hope this letter encourages reflection, accountability, and meaningful change within the Nursing Department of José Rizal University.Respectfully,A Concerned Nursing Student

Ikaw pa nga mismo ang nagsasabi na kapag nahihirapan kami, sabihin lang sa’yo. Pero kapag may nagsabi na, ikaw pa ang nagagalit. Nagagalit ka kapag may slow learner sa klase? Take Accountability and Be professionalFor my longest time here in Jose Rizal University—from grade school to college. I’ve honestly seen it all. But I was still surprised by how the heads acted during earlier’s FGD.I was closely listening to each concern and suggestion per block of this year’s BSN first years. I witnessed repetitive feedback, from General subjects to our very own specialized ones.Hanggang sa, hala, bigla silang nag-surprise recitation just to—what—prove a point na "walang natutunan"? I tried to fully grasp their situation. I can also see the recent post here defending sir.To those who are curious: Prof din po namin si sir, and honestly, he is one of the coolest and most laid-back person you will ever know. During lectures, all of his words are so knowledge-filled that you can see why he truly deserves his Master’s degree and all those additional letters after his name to prove his competence.Now, now! We all know professors can see this. We do not want this to become a feud between anyone. Please do not make this into a toxic workplace beef between you and the said professor.May point naman sila ma’am, TBH. Maximize daw dapat ang time and indulge in activities to create retention and understanding. Hello? Teach-back method, indulge in interactive activities. NGL, at one point naisip ko, "oo nga naman."BUT? Haha. In other subjects kung saan sinasabi na may problem sa pagtuturo ang teacher, ang sagot ay mag-self-study raw kasi iba pa rin ang personal na aralin. Meanwhile, in Anaphy—where we seek more time for self-study kasi naibigay na ang knowledge and need na lang namin mai-absorb at mag-perform ng learning methods na gagana sa amin. Ayaw naman?Saka, if you would like to have retention, bakit ninyo ginawang 10 hours sa isang araw, ma? Sana ginawa ninyong 3 hours per day.We know na medyo lacking kayo sa professors at kino-compress ninyo silang lahat, so schedules are really tight.Again, please try to be more professional and nice—kahit kitang-kita na sa mukha at singhal ninyo how you judge student questions. Na para bang "Anong tanong 'to? Ang gulo naman magtanong nito" 'yung nakasulat sa faces ninyo.Ang gulo naman talaga, lol. They’re sugarcoating their words kasi. Sana kasi diniretso ninyo na lang na: "Nag-enroll at nagbabayad ako para matuto from professional health educators. Hindi para sabihin sa akin ng professor na mag-aral ako nang wala siyang tinuturo at magbasa lang sa PPT na gawa niya at syllabus?!"And 'di ba nga, concern nga ito? Don't take it too personally just to prove your point. It could have been handled nicely.'Yung may problema, dedepensahan ninyo. 'Yung walang problema, kinakalaban ninyo.

𝐓𝐇𝐄 𝐄𝐗𝐓𝐑𝐀 𝐅𝐈𝐕𝐄 𝐓𝐇𝐀𝐓 𝐆𝐎𝐓 𝐀𝐖𝐀𝐘 ⏱One possession away from victory, the JRU Light Bombers saw their early advantage slip away as the La Salle Green Hills Greenies pulled off an 89–88 overtime comeback in the NCAA Season 102 Juniors' Basketball Tournament on November 6 at the Playtime FilOil Centre in San Juan City.Lorenz Cinco paced the Blue and Gold with 28 points and 5 rebounds, while JC Cruz added 19 points and 8 boards. James Manlapaz and Paul Navera chipped in 11 points apiece to fuel JRU's offensive effort.On the defensive end, Justine Santos contributed 12 rebounds and 5 blocks, while Luis Lugtu recorded 7 assists.JRU opened the game with a strong first quarter, taking a 27–16 lead. LSGH fought back in the second, scoring 17 points to JRU's 15 and slowly cutting into the lead.The Greenies took advantage of their momentum in the third, holding the Light Bombers to just 11 points while putting up 22 of their own. JRU answered in the fourth, pouring in 25 points against LSGH's 23 to knot the score at 78 and force an extra five minutes.With the game hanging in the balance, the Light Bombers appeared to have the upper hand after building an 88–82 cushion with 45 seconds left in overtime. But LSGH refused to go quietly, putting together a late scoring run to bring the game within reach.The final two seconds proved decisive, as Paul Navera sank a crucial free throw to hand the Greenies an 89–88 lead. The late conversion completed LSGH's comeback and left the Light Bombers just short of the win.The loss dropped the Light Bombers to a 10–3 record in Group A, but JRU remained at the top of the standings, keeping its No. 1 seed and twice-to-beat advantage heading into the quarterfinals. Despite the setback, the Blue and Gold have already secured their place in the next round.Although the final score did not fall in their favor, the Light Bombers' fight from the opening tip to the final possession showed that their campaign remains far from over as they turn their attention to the next stage of the tournament.Photos by: Kyrie Bago | Article by: Cassandra Albuna#JRULightBombers #NCAASeason102
